passages.t: A house built, and a heart that aches
passages.happening:
‘Every wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands’ (verse 1). ‘Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox’ (verse 4).

There are sayings on honest witnesses and on the mocker who looks for wisdom and cannot find it (verses 5-6). ‘Stay away from a foolish man; you will gain no knowledge from his speech’ (verse 7).

Then the chapter turns inward. ‘The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy’ (verse 10). “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death” (verse 12). ‘Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in sorrow’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The opening chapters ended with Wisdom building her house on seven pillars, and Folly sitting at her door (9:1, 13). Verse 1 brings that picture down to ordinary life. Every wise woman builds her house. The book is showing what it looks like to accept Wisdom's invitation.

Verse 4 is a farmer's observation. An ox eats, needs care and dirties the stall, and a family might be tempted to keep the manger clean by keeping no ox. But without the ox there is no plowing and no harvest. A fruitful life is messy. Refusing the mess means refusing the fruit.

Verses 10 to 14 look into the heart. No one else can fully share another person's bitterness or joy. Laughter can cover an ache. And people can deceive themselves: a road can seem right and still lead to death. The same line comes again, word for word, at 16:25.
passages.later: Hannah knew the bitterness verse 10 describes: ‘In her bitter distress, Hannah prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears’ (1 Samuel 1:10). She took it to the LORD, who sees what no stranger can.
passages.asks: No one else can fully know your heart's bitterness, but God can. Ask what you are carrying behind a smile, and whether you have brought it to him. And ask whether any road you are on seems right only because you have not looked at where it ends.

passages.t: The simple, the prudent, and the poor man's neighbors
passages.happening:
‘The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps’ (verse 15). ‘A wise man fears and turns from evil, but a fool is careless and reckless’ (verse 16). ‘A quick-tempered man acts foolishly’ (verse 17).

Then two sayings side by side. ‘The poor man is hated even by his neighbor, but many are those who love the rich’ (verse 20). ‘He who despises his neighbor sins, but blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor’ (verse 21).

‘Do not those who contrive evil go astray? But those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness’ (verse 22). ‘There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Verses 15 to 18 contrast the simple and the prudent. The simple are not wicked. They are naive, believing whatever they are told. The prudent look before they step.

Verse 22 is phrased as a question, which is rare in this collection. The reader is invited to supply the answer.

Verses 20 and 21 must be read together. The first tells the truth about human behavior. The second tells the truth about God's judgment on it.
passages.later: Job felt verse 20 from the inside: ‘My kinsmen have failed me, and my friends have forgotten me’ (Job 19:14). And John asks, ‘If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?’ (1 John 3:17).
passages.hard:
Verse 20 says the poor are hated even by their neighbors while the rich have many friends. Is Proverbs approving of that?

No. Many sayings in Proverbs are observations, not commands, and verse 20 is one of them. It reports what everyone can see: wealth attracts company and poverty drives it away. The book says similar things elsewhere (19:4, 7). A reader who takes every saying as moral advice will misread it badly.

The very next verse gives the verdict: ‘He who despises his neighbor sins’ (verse 21). Putting the two sayings side by side is part of the teaching.

This matters for reading the whole collection. Proverbs describes the world as it usually works, its injustices included, and trusts the reader to tell description from instruction. Some sayings commend, some warn, and some simply observe so that the wise will not be naive. The bribe that opens doors in 17:8 is another example. None of them gives anyone a reason to look down on the poor.
passages.asks: The poor man's neighbor turned away. Ask who near you is easy to overlook because they have little to offer. And ask what one kindness would look like this week, since verse 21 calls it the opposite of sin.

passages.t: A fountain of life, and the poor man's Maker
passages.happening:
‘A truthful witness saves lives’ (verse 25). ‘He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge’ (verse 26). ‘The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death’ (verse 27).

‘A patient man has great understanding, but a quick-tempered man promotes folly’ (verse 29). ‘A tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones’ (verse 30).

“Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him” (verse 31). ‘The righteous man has a refuge even in death’ (verse 32). ‘Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people’ (verse 34). And ‘A king delights in a wise servant’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Verse 31 rests on the belief, rooted in Genesis 1, that God made every human being. To crush the poor is not only a social wrong. It is an insult thrown at the one who made them. Kindness to the needy honors him. The theme comes back in 17:5 and 22:2.

Verses 28 and 35 assume a king. A king's splendor lay in his people, who meant farmers, soldiers and taxes, and a ruler without subjects had nothing to rule. Kings relied on servants and officials who could make or break a reign.

Verse 34 speaks of any people or nation. The Hebrew word is general, not Israel alone. Proverbs speaks to human beings as such: righteousness and sin shape the fortunes of every people. It is a word about any nation's conduct, not a promise to any one nation.
passages.later: The poor man's dignity rests on the first chapter of the Bible: ‘So God created man in His own image’ (Genesis 1:27). And James gives the same counsel as verse 29: ‘Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger’ (James 1:19).
passages.asks: Verse 31 says the way you treat the poor is the way you treat their Maker. Ask how you speak of the poor, and how you treat them when no one is watching. And ask what envy may be rotting in you, and what a tranquil heart would look like instead.
